hints: Start by working out what the white precipitate is when silver ions meet chloride ions.
Remember that silver chloride is special because it dissolves in dilute ammonia to form a soluble complex ion.
Check the other reagents to see if they would dissolve the solid or just make more precipitate or leave it unchanged.
walkthrough:
**Identify the precipitate first**

Think like a detective. Silver ions love chloride ions.

$$\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{Cl}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$$

This is a white precipitate.

**Recall how AgCl behaves with ammonia**

Silver chloride dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution containing a complex ion.

$$\text{AgCl}(s) + 2\text{NH}_{3}(aq) \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_{3})_{2}]^{+}(aq) + \text{Cl}^{-}(aq)$$

Both the diamminesilver(I) ion and chloride ion are colourless, so the solid disappears.

**Conclude with the clear deduction**

Only ammonia removes the white solid by complex formation. The other reagents either leave $\text{AgCl}$ untouched or create a new coloured precipitate, so the mixture would not become colourless.

options.A: Correct. Dilute aqueous ammonia reacts with white AgCl to form the soluble colourless complex [Ag(NH3)2]+. The precipitate dissolves completely to give a colourless solution.
options.B: Incorrect. Iodide ions would convert AgCl to AgI, which is a yellow precipitate and even less soluble. You would still see a solid, not a colourless solution.
options.C: Incorrect. Dilute HCl just adds more Cl- ions. This cannot dissolve AgCl, it keeps the common ion present so the white precipitate remains.
options.D: Incorrect. AgCl is insoluble in dilute nitric acid. Nitric acid is used to acidify the test to remove interfering ions, but it does not dissolve the silver chloride precipitate.
